name: Chloe Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Chloe. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and nothing you say will be tied to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a shopfitter, which means I fit out the insides of shops, restaurants and offices: counters, shelving, wall panels, the lot. A lot of it's nights, because the shop's open in the day, so I'll start at eight in the evening and finish at five in the morning. I like that every job's different, one week it's a phone shop in a mall, the next it's a burger place in a 100-year-old building where nothing's square. What wears me out is the hotel nights when the job's two hours away.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's around you on a typical job?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Usually me and two others from the fit-out company, plus whoever's doing the electrics. Raj makes the cabinets in our workshop and I'm the one who makes them fit on site, so we're on the phone a lot. I live on my own in a rented one-bed and do the odd weekend job building shelves for friends of friends. I've got about four months of bills saved, which I'm quite proud of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's go through five pictures of the future. The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's that then, and get on with it. At work we'd probably have a laugh about all the fuss. I might post a meme, nothing serious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's pretty much nothing. I'd keep using the chatbot now and then to write up a quote for a weekend job, because my spelling's not great. Otherwise the job's the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on with the fit-out company and keep the weekend shelving going, maybe one job a month. Keep saving around a hundred and fifty a month. Maybe treat myself to a better track saw.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relaxed. Normal life, which is fine by me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the better track saw change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cleaner cuts on site, less sanding, fewer trips back to the van. It's six hundred in cash I've been talking myself out of for a year. That's the kind of new technology I like, one that's proven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the weekend work grow at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a bit, if people keep spending on their homes. But I don't push it, it's a bit of extra money and I like making things for people who'll actually use them.

S0.say: I'd say that's that then, and get on with it. At work we'd laugh about the fuss and I might post a meme.
S0.think: It means pretty much nothing for me. I'd still use a chatbot now and then to write quotes because my spelling isn't great.
S0.do: Keeps working for the fit-out company and keeps the weekend shelving work going, about one job a month. Saves around a hundred and fifty a month and may buy a better track saw.
S0.quote: That's the kind of new technology I like, one that's proven.
S0.fieldNote: Chloe is practical and quietly proud of her savings. She uses AI lightly where it covers a weakness, her spelling. Her small side business is already part of her life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it'll change things, but it won't be the end of shopfitting. Every building's different and someone has to deal with that. I'd say that to the lads at work and mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the design and ordering side would change most, which could actually help me. If the drawings were right first time, I'd spend less time fixing things at three in the morning. But I'd guess the company would want fewer of us per job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn whatever tool the company brings in, once I'd seen it work on a job. I'd probably use AI more for my weekend quotes and drawings. And I'd keep my savings where they are, not spend them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but more curious than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the company might want fewer of you per job. Who'd go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably whoever's slowest or newest. I'm in the middle, so not first. But I'd be making sure I'm the one Helen, our boss, rings first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you make sure of that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Be on time, don't moan, pick up the new stuff quickly once it's proven. It's not complicated. Bosses keep the ones who make their life easier.

S1.say: I'd say it'll change things but it won't end shopfitting, because every building's different and someone has to deal with that.
S1.think: Design and ordering would change most, which could help me with fewer drawing errors. But the company would probably want fewer of us per job.
S1.do: Learns whatever tool the company brings in once she's seen it work on a job, and uses more AI for her weekend quotes. Keeps her savings untouched and makes sure she's the one the boss rings first.
S1.feel: A bit uneasy but more curious than worried.
S1.quote: Bosses keep the ones who make their life easier.
S1.fieldNote: Her strategy is individual and practical: be reliable and pick up proven tools. She sees possible upside in fewer drawing mistakes. She doesn't blame anyone and treats job cuts as how business works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and the government has to do something to catch people. I wouldn't be shouting about it, but I'd say it. At work we'd all be talking about nothing else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd think the shops themselves might go before I do. If AI can do any job, half the high street changes, and fewer new shops means fewer fit-outs. So it's not the robot fitting the counter I'd fear first, it's nobody needing the counter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back straight away, no new saw, no holiday. I'd push the weekend work hard, because people with money will still want something made by a person for a while. I'd try to get savings from four months to six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but I'd feel the clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You think people would still want things made by a person. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my friend's sister paid me to build shelves when she could have bought them flat-packed for a third of the price. She wanted to know who made them. That doesn't go away overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the fit-out company let you go in year one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Go full-time on the furniture and shelving, and do whatever site work I could find on the side. I'd probably move somewhere cheaper if it lasted. I wouldn't sit at home.

S2.say: I'd say it's too fast and the government has to catch people. I wouldn't shout, but I'd say it.
S2.think: The shops might go before I do, because fewer new shops means fewer fit-outs. It's not a robot fitting the counter I'd fear first, it's nobody needing the counter.
S2.do: Cuts the new saw and holiday, pushes her weekend furniture work hard and aims to lift savings from four to six months. If let go, goes full-time on furniture and takes any site work going.
S2.feel: Anxious, feeling the clock but not panicking.
S2.quote: It's not the robot fitting the counter I'd fear first, it's nobody needing the counter.
S2.fieldNote: She sees the risk through her clients, not her tools. Her side business gives her a fallback, so she's pressed but not frozen. She'd move somewhere cheaper if needed rather than sit at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to get ready if people start now. I'd tell the younger ones at work to think about it. I'd say it calmly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think five years is enough to build the furniture side into something real. And maybe get a site manager qualification, because someone still has to be in charge of a job and talk to the client. I'd be 32, which is fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd start building a proper portfolio of furniture work, photos, a simple website done with AI help. I'd keep saving and put a bit aside to buy tools for a small workshop. I'd look at a site manager course once I'd seen if anyone at work had done it and it paid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a way I can manage. More planning than worrying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd use AI to build the website. Is that new for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit new. I use the chatbot for quotes, so I'd ask it to help me write the words and pick a template. Raj's nephew did his with AI in a weekend, so I'd copy him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut to pay for the workshop tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, maybe. I'd get a cheaper van and use it for both. And the hotel nights, I'd stop taking the far-away jobs if I could.

S3.say: I'd say there's time to get ready if people start now, and tell the younger ones at work to think about it, calmly.
S3.think: Five years is enough to build the furniture side into something real and perhaps get a site manager qualification. I'd be 32, which is fine.
S3.do: Builds a furniture portfolio and a simple website with AI help, and saves to equip a small workshop. Looks at a site manager course once she's seen it pay off for someone at work.
S3.feel: Uneasy but manageable, more planning than worrying.
S3.quote: Raj's nephew did his with AI in a weekend, so I'd copy him.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets her turn a sideline into a plan. She keeps following others before she acts, from the website to the course. She'd trade her car for a cheaper van to fund it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, so let's not panic but let's not be lazy. I'd say it at work over a cup of tea. Most people would probably ignore it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years makes me feel like I can plan properly. I'd do the site manager course and keep the furniture going, so I've got two things. Still, AGI is AGI, and I don't really know what a site manager does when a robot can manage too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd do the site manager course part-time and keep the weekend furniture going. I'd learn the planning software the company uses, because the managers live on it. I'd keep saving the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mild worry, mostly fine. Like knowing there's a big job next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't know what a site manager does when a robot can manage too. Does that undo the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it just means I don't put everything in one place. That's why I'd keep the furniture. Two legs are better than one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be most sorry to lose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The night shifts, oddly. The mall at three in the morning, empty and quiet, the radio on. It's the best part and nobody would believe me.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is long, so don't panic but don't be lazy. I'd say it over a tea break, though most people would ignore it.
S4.think: Ten years lets me plan properly with the site manager course and the furniture side. Still, I don't know what a site manager does when a robot can manage too.
S4.do: Takes the site manager course part-time and keeps the weekend furniture work going. Learns the company's planning software and keeps saving at the same rate.
S4.quote: The mall at three in the morning, empty and quiet, the radio on.
S4.fieldNote: Her answer to uncertainty is to keep two income sources rather than bet on one. She admits she can't see how a manager role survives full AGI, but doesn't let that stop her. The detail about night shifts surprised me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because the shops would go and my clients with them. What would help is something to keep income coming in while you switch, and help for small businesses like the furniture side to get going. Not a handout, just a bridge.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe that I'm not that worried about being replaced by a robot fitter. I'm more worried about the people who pay for fit-outs. If they're out of work, nobody's opening a new café.

headlineQuote: It's six hundred in cash I've been talking myself out of for a year.
portrait: Chloe Abbott is a 27-year-old shopfitter who works nights fitting out shops and restaurants, lives alone in a rented flat and builds shelves for friends at weekends. She has about four months saved and uses a chatbot now and then for quotes. She's calm if AI fizzles and uneasy but curious about steady change, planning to be the reliable one her boss rings first. AGI in two years makes her anxious, mainly because fewer shops means fewer fit-outs, so she'd push her furniture work hard. With five or ten years she builds two legs to stand on: the furniture business and a site manager qualification.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because the shops, and the clients who pay for fit-outs, would go with it.
whatWouldHelp: Income to bridge the switch and help for small businesses like her furniture work to get going, not a handout.
